places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Refounded as the colony Aelia Capitolina in 130 and called that in official use for four centuries; the old name never stopped being used by the people who lived there.

places.name: Gaza
places.note: The Persian loanword *gaza*, a royal treasury, is a homonym and has nothing to do with the city; Acts 8 puts the two in one sentence.

places.name: Caesarea
places.note: Herod's harbour city, the Roman and then the Byzantine capital of the province -- not a bishopric of the second rank until Jerusalem overtook it.

places.name: the Holy Sepulchre
places.note: One building for four purposes -- tomb, rock of the crucifixion, Constantinian basilica, and the address at which every dispute over the holy places has been conducted since.

places.name: Mar Saba
places.note: Continuously inhabited since 483, which makes it the oldest occupied monastery in Palestine and one of the oldest anywhere.

places.name: Ramla
places.note: The one city in Palestine founded by Muslims, and for three centuries the administrative capital of the province -- which is why so much of the Christian record after 715 is written from a town with no biblical past at all.

places.name: the Marneion
places.note: The great temple of Gaza and the church Porphyry built over it are one site; the pin is the best guess, since neither has been excavated with certainty under the modern city.

places.name: Sinai
places.note: Pinned at the monastery. The peninsula and the mountain carry the same name in the sources and are seldom distinguished.

places.name: Pella
places.note: The town the Jerusalem church is said to have fled to before the war of 66-70. Whether the flight happened as Eusebius reports it is the most argued sentence in the first part of this book.

places.name: the Holy Family
places.note: The Latin parish in Zeitoun, the second of Gaza's two functioning churches and the other of its two wartime refuges.

places.name: Maiumas
places.note: Gaza's port, made a city in its own right under Constantine and named Constantia -- then demoted back to a suburb by Julian. Two towns, four miles apart, with two bishops and one quarrel.

places.name: Azotus
places.note: Ancient Azotus is the tell inland; the modern city of the name is a twentieth-century port some kilometres north.

places.name: Thabatha
places.note: Hilarion's village south of Gaza; the monastery excavated at Umm el-Amr is the best candidate for his own, and it is the earliest monastic site in Palestine.

places.name: Mamilla
places.note: The pool outside the western wall where the Persian sack of 614 is said to have ended; the number of the dead reported there is the most contested figure in the book.

places.name: St Porphyrius
places.note: The oldest church still in use in Gaza, holding the relics of the bishop who destroyed the Marneion; it gave refuge to Christians and Muslims alike in the war after 2023 and was struck in October of that year.

places.name: Phaeno
places.note: The imperial copper mines of Arabia, where confessors were sent maimed rather than killed -- a sentence the Palestinian church remembered by name for centuries.

places.name: Mamre
places.note: A fair, a pagan shrine, a Jewish tradition and a Constantinian basilica on one enclosure -- the clearest single case in Palestine of a holy place changing hands without changing address.

places.name: Ḥamāma
places.note: Depopulated in 1948.

places.name: Bethar
places.note: Where the second revolt ended in 135, and with it the last Jewish Jerusalem the church of the circumcision belonged to.

places.name: Iqrit
places.note: Depopulated in 1948 and never resettled; the church still stands and the community still buries its dead there.

places.name: the Deir al-Sultan
places.note: A courtyard and a set of cells on the roof of the Holy Sepulchre, held by the Ethiopians and claimed by the Copts, and the smallest and most persistent of the disputes over the holy places.

places.name: Meroë
places.note: The eunuch's kingdom on the upper Nile, in what is now northern Sudan -- not the modern country called Ethiopia, which the Greek *Aithiops* never meant.

places.name: Nessana
places.note: The papyri found in its church in 1935 are the fullest surviving record of ordinary Christian life in Palestine across the Arab conquest -- the same families, the same church, before and after.

places.name: Dayr al-Shaykh
places.note: Depopulated in 1948.

places.name: Beit Affa
places.note: Depopulated in 1948.

routes.name: The Gaza road
routes.note: The road of Acts 8, and the book's own through-line. Which of the roads down from Jerusalem Luke meant is disputed -- the southern one through the dry hills rather than the busy one through Lydda -- and the line drawn here takes that reading.

routes.name: Fabri's contracted road
routes.note: Felix Fabri's pilgrim party of 1483 contracted for the desert crossing at Gaza; the price, the camels and the escort are all in his account.

routes.name: The flight to Pella
routes.note: Eusebius reports that the Jerusalem church left the city for Pella before the war of 66-70. The line is drawn because the book argues about it, not because the journey is documented.
